Section Labels: Naming the Parts of a Song

When you map a recording in the Timestamp Notes, S stamps a section and gives it a label from a menu. This lesson covers what each label means, when to use letters instead of words, and how the page counts the choruses each player takes.

Two kinds of stamp

  • S marks a section: the place where a new part of the form starts. It gets a label from the menu, and the bar map, the chord grid, the phrases and Send on all use it.
  • C marks a note: anything else worth finding again (“drum fill”, “key change”, “wrong note at 1:12”). A note is just text, and it doesn’t split the song into sections.

Both kinds of stamp go in the same Timestamps list, in time order. Section stamps are tinted blue and have the menu.

The words

Label What it is Where you hear it
Intro Music before the first real section, often a vamp or the last bars of the tune Pop, rock, jazz
Head The tune itself, played straight through, before and after the solos Jazz
Verse Words that change each time over the same music Songs
Pre-chorus A short build that lifts the verse into the chorus Pop
Chorus The part that comes back with the same words: the hook Songs
Bridge Contrasting music, usually heard once or twice Songs, jazz (the B of AABA)
Interlude An instrumental passage between sung sections Songs
Solo One player improvising over the form. Choose the instrument (Sax solo, Piano solo…) Jazz, rock
Shout A written ensemble chorus, the whole band loud together, often after the solos Big band, small group arrangements
Outro Whatever comes after the last real section: a tag, a vamp, a fade Everywhere

The same word in pop and in jazz can mean different things. In a song a chorus is a section with the hook. In jazz a chorus is one time through the whole form: “he took three choruses” means the soloist went through the form three times.

The letters

Jazz standards and older songs are usually described by form letters: each new piece of music gets the next letter, and a piece that comes back gets its old letter.

  • AABA (32 bars, 8 each): I Got Rhythm, Satin Doll. The B is the bridge.
  • ABAC: All of Me. The second A returns, but the end goes somewhere new.
  • A A′: the A comes back with a different ending. A′ (“A prime”) means nearly A.

The menu starts by offering A. Once you’ve used A, it also offers A′ (A changed) and B (something new). Each letter you use adds the next one: B brings B′ and C, A′ brings A″. You never have to type a prime mark.

Letters aren’t numbered. An AABA tune should have three A’s, so they all stay “A”.

Numbering is automatic

Pick the same word twice and both are numbered: two Heads become Head 1 and Head 2 everywhere they appear (the bar map, the chord grid, the Notation page). Delete one and the other goes back to plain Head. Move a stamp earlier and the numbers follow time order, not the order you stamped them.

Need a label that isn’t on the menu? Choose Other… at the bottom and type it (“Vamp”, “Drum break”, “Trading 4s”). A typed label is kept exactly as you wrote it. The ▾ next to it takes you back to the menu.

Choruses: who soloed how long

Once the bars are tapped (B), the page measures each section and divides it by the length of one chorus:

  • One chorus is the length of the first Head stamp. If you stamped letters, it’s the A A B A (or whatever pattern repeats). If the guess is wrong, type the bar count into a chorus is __ bars.
  • Back-to-back stamps with the same label are one solo. It doesn’t matter whether you stamp the sax solo once or at the top of every chorus: three stamps of Sax solo, 32 bars each, make Sax 3 choruses.
  • Untapped bars are worked out from the tempo, so you can tap one chorus, stamp the rest with S and still get a count. The last section runs to the end of the recording.
  • A count of 1.5 means the solo stopped halfway through the form. That happens, but check that your stamp is in the right place.

In a song (no Head and no letters), sections can each be a different length, so a solo is counted in bars instead, along with the section it matches in length: “Guitar 8 bars (as long as the Verse)”. A last chorus tapped twice as long as the first plays its chords through twice rather than holding each one twice as long. If one section is a bar over a multiple of four and the next is a bar under (9 then 7), the Sections panel marks both with ⚠: one stamp is probably a bar off.

Fill from the tempo (in the Bar map panel) goes further: tap the head, stamp where each solo starts, and it puts in every bar after the taps. Between two stamps the bars are spread evenly, so a band that speeds up or slows down lands back on each stamp. A head or solo that comes out within about a tenth of a chorus of a whole number becomes that many choruses. The guessed bars are grey in the Bars table. Tap B on any downbeat where they drift: your tap is kept and the bars around it are worked out again. Clear guesses takes them all out.

Each count appears next to the solo’s first stamp, and the full list is under the Timestamps.

Example: Beautiful Love, McCoy Tyner Quartet

Beautiful Love (Victor Young) has 32 bars in two 16-bar halves. The second half is the same as the first until its ending, so its form is A A′. In a quartet recording you might stamp:

Time S label Shown as
0:01 Head Head 1
0:52 Sax solo Sax solo
1:43 Sax solo Sax solo
2:34 Piano solo Piano solo
4:15 Head Head 2

Head 1 is 32 bars, so a chorus is 32 bars. The two sax stamps together are 64 bars, so the list shows Sax 2 choruses.

You can also stamp each half: A at 0:01, A′ at 0:26. The page then finds that A A′ repeats and uses its 32 bars as one chorus.

Exercise

  1. Choose a jazz recording with a head and at least two solos.
  2. Listen once and press S each time the form starts again. Choose Head, then the soloists.
  3. Tap a chorus of bars (B).
  4. Read the chorus counts. Do they match what you heard? If a count is a half, find the stamp that’s off.
  5. Do it again with letters only (A, A, B, A…) and check that the chorus length comes out the same.
